GESTRA

Real-Time Sign Language Translation and Two-Way Communication System

How a conversation flows

The problem

People who are deaf or mute often struggle to communicate in real-time conversations. Existing solutions are either too expensive, require internet, or are not portable. Gestra provides an affordable, offline, wearable solution.

Expensive Needs internet Not portable

Solution : Gestra

Gestra is a wearable real-time two-way communication device that helps people who cannot speak or hear. It features a gesture-to-text translation process and a speech-to-text translation process, running through microcontrollers and an Android app — so a conversation can flow in both directions between a deaf or mute person and a hearing person, without either side needing to know sign language.

Gestra — affordable Gestra — offline Gestra — wearable

Right Glove

4× flex / force sensors
MPU6050 motion IMU
ESP32-C3 controller
OLED display

Gesture → text

The Right Glove uses four flex/force sensors on the fingers and an MPU6050 for detecting movement of the whole hand. Pressing a finger and holding it for 2 seconds makes the OLED display the word assigned to that specific sensor. Moving the hand up, down, left, or right also displays a word. As a safety feature, holding the index finger press longer (7 seconds total) triggers an emergency alert, which sends an SMS to the emergency contact.

Left Glove

INMP441 I2S microphone
ESP32-S3 controller
Vosk offline speech-to-text
Screen readout

Speech → text

The Left Glove uses a small microphone to pick up spoken words, and an ESP32 sends the audio wirelessly to an Android app, where the app converts the audio into text using offline speech recognition (Vosk). The text is then sent back and displayed on a small screen, so anything spoken is turned into readable words in near real-time — without needing an internet connection.

App & dashboard

Android app

The Gestra Android app is the user's control center. It displays speech translations, keeps a history of past conversations, and shows the connection status of both wearable devices. All the word mappings for the gestures are customizable through the app. It also manages emergency contacts with SMS alerts and quick-dial options.

The app uses a foreground service, so it continues running in the background and staying connected to the ESP32 even when the phone screen is off.

Web dashboard

Alongside the app, a web dashboard gives guardians or family remote visibility, a live emergency alert banner, real-time location tracking on a map, and a live transcript feed — so they can monitor the user's safety and communication from anywhere.

Firebase

Firebase acts as the bridge between the app and the web dashboard. When the app sends data like emergency alerts, live transcripts, or GPS location, it gets pushed to Firebase. The web dashboard is connected to the same Firebase database, so it updates automatically the moment new data arrives, without needing to refresh the page.

Power system

The power supply is built around a rechargeable 3.7V LiPo battery, charged safely through a TP4056 charging module. Since the ESP32 needs 5V, an MT3608 boost converter steps the battery's voltage up before it reaches the board. The battery connects via a removable JST connector, and an ON/OFF switch lets you power the system down without unplugging anything.

Components

MPU6050 Motion Tracking Sensor
A 6-axis IMU combining a 3-axis accelerometer and 3-axis gyroscope. It detects orientation, tilt, acceleration, and rotational movement — useful for motion gestures, stability detection, or tracking how a device is being moved or held.
Force Sensitive Sensors
Detect pressure or force applied to a surface by changing resistance under load. Used to sense touch intensity, grip strength, or weight/contact detection.
ESP32-S3 Super Mini
A compact microcontroller board with WiFi + Bluetooth, dual-core processing, and AI acceleration support. The brain of the Left Glove — handles sensor fusion, logic, and communication, since it has more processing power and often more RAM/PSRAM than the C3.
ESP32-C3 Super Mini
A smaller, single-core RISC-V microcontroller with WiFi + Bluetooth Low Energy. The brain of the Right Glove, usually used for a lighter task — it's cheaper and less powerful than the S3.
INMP441 Microphone
A digital I2S MEMS microphone. Captures audio input digitally (no need for an analog-to-digital converter), commonly used for voice capture in speech recognition projects.
OLED Display
A small, low-power screen. Used to show status info, menus, sensor readings, or feedback text to the user.
Vosk Offline Speech Recognition API
An offline speech-to-text engine that runs without internet access. Converts captured audio (e.g. from the INMP441) into text locally — useful for privacy-friendly or no-connectivity voice command systems.
TP4056 Charging Module
A single-cell lithium battery charging circuit (via USB-C). Manages safe charging of the 3.7V LiPo battery and often includes protection circuitry against overcharge/overdischarge.
MT3608 Booster Module
A DC-DC step-up boost converter. Takes the battery's 3.7V and boosts it to a higher, stable voltage like 5V for components that require more voltage than the battery alone provides.
3.7V LiPo Battery
A rechargeable lithium-polymer battery — the portable power source for the whole system.
